lines.content: HRvest is a desktop address book for hiring managers at startups who track candidates through the hiring pipeline. Every action is a short typed command, so an experienced user can work faster than they would in a mouse-driven applicant tracking system.
* Stores each candidate's contact details, roles, current pipeline status, note, and tags in HRvest.

* Supports commands to add, edit, delete, list, find, filter by status or role, add notes, update status, view a candidate in full (`expand`), manage the role catalog, import and export candidates as CSV, clear all records, exit, and open help.
* Saves candidates and roles as JSON files in a `data` folder in the folder you run HRvest from. No cloud account, database, or network connection.

A hiring manager at a tech startup who manages 10 to 50 candidates at a time for 1 to 3 open roles, prefers typing over clicking, and finds most enterprise applicant tracking systems too slow for day-to-day pipeline updates.
See [Setting up and getting started](docs/SettingUp.md) for prerequisites and local build instructions.
For end-user command reference and feature details, see the [HRvest User Guide](docs/UserGuide.md). For architecture and extension notes, see the [Developer Guide](docs/DeveloperGuide.md).

HRvest is based on the [AddressBook-Level3 project](https://github.com/se-edu/addressbook-level3) by the [SE-EDU initiative](https://se-education.org). The AB3 codebase gives us the model, logic, and storage layers that HRvest extends.

* HRvest is based on [AddressBook-Level3](https://github.com/se-edu/addressbook-level3) (AB3) by the SE-EDU initiative. HRvest keeps AB3's architecture, and parts of its code, documentation and diagrams are adapted from AB3.
* HRvest uses [JavaFX](https://openjfx.io/) for its GUI, [Jackson](https://github.com/FasterXML/jackson) for JSON and CSV tag data, and [JUnit 5](https://junit.org/junit5/) for testing.
* Team members used AI coding assistants for parts of the code, tests and documentation, guided by the repository's `AGENTS.md`.
Refer to the guide [_Setting up and getting started_](SettingUp.md).

The following provides a quick overview of the main components and their interactions.

**`Main`** (consisting of classes [`Main`](https://github.com/AY2627S1-CS2103-F10-1/tp/tree/master/src/main/java/seedu/address/Main.java) and [`MainApp`](https://github.com/AY2627S1-CS2103-F10-1/tp/tree/master/src/main/java/seedu/address/MainApp.java)) is in charge of the app launch and shut down.
* At app launch, it initializes the other components in the correct sequence, and connects them up with each other.
* At shut down, it shuts down the other components and invokes cleanup methods where necessary.
The bulk of the app's work is done by the following four components:
* [**`Model`**](#model-component): Holds the data of the App in memory.
* [**`Storage`**](#storage-component): Reads data from, and writes data to, the hard disk.
[**`Commons`**](#common-classes) represents a collection of classes used by multiple other components.
**How the architecture components interact with each other**
The *Sequence Diagram* below shows how the components interact with each other for the scenario where the user issues the command `delete 1`.
Each of the four main components (also shown in the diagram above),
* defines its *API* in an `interface` with the same name as the Component.
* provides its functionality through a concrete `{Component Name}Manager` class that implements the corresponding API interface.

For example, the `Logic` component defines its API in `Logic.java` and implements it in `LogicManager.java`. Other components interact with a component through its interface rather than its concrete class, preventing them from coupling to that component's implementation, as illustrated in the following partial class diagram.
The sections below give more details of each component.
The **API** of this component is specified in [`Ui.java`](https://github.com/AY2627S1-CS2103-F10-1/tp/tree/master/src/main/java/seedu/address/ui/Ui.java)

The UI consists of a `MainWindow` and its parts, such as `CandidateSummaryHeader`, `CommandBox`, `ResultDisplay`, `PersonListPanel`, and `StatusBarFooter`. These UI parts, including `MainWindow`, inherit from the abstract `UiPart` class, which captures common behavior among classes that represent visible GUI parts.

The following diagram details `CandidateSummaryHeader`, which composes the top row from an `AppLogo` and a group of summary cards: one `CandidateSummaryCard` for all candidates and a `StatusSummaryCard` for each recruitment status. These parts also inherit from `UiPart`.
<puml src="diagrams/CandidateSummaryHeaderClassDiagram.puml" alt="Structure of the candidate summary header"/>

The `UI` component uses the JavaFX UI framework. The layouts of these UI parts are defined in matching `.fxml` files in `src/main/resources/view`. For example, [`MainWindow.fxml`](https://github.com/AY2627S1-CS2103-F10-1/tp/tree/master/src/main/resources/view/MainWindow.fxml) specifies the layout of [`MainWindow`](https://github.com/AY2627S1-CS2103-F10-1/tp/tree/master/src/main/java/seedu/address/ui/MainWindow.java).
* executes user commands using the `Logic` component.
* listens for changes to `Model` data so that the UI can be updated with the modified data.
* keeps a reference to the `Logic` component, because the `UI` relies on the `Logic` to execute commands.
* depends on some classes in the `Model` component because it displays `Person` objects from the model.

1. When `Logic` is called upon to execute a command, the command is passed to an `AddressBookParser` object, which in turn creates a parser that matches the command (e.g., `DeleteCommandParser`) and uses it to parse the command.
1. This results in a `Command` object (more precisely, an object of one of its subclasses e.g., `DeleteCommand`) which is executed by the `LogicManager`.
1. The command can communicate with the `Model` when it is executed (e.g. to delete a candidate).
For `delete 1`, the command first gets the displayed list from the `Model`, then deletes the candidate `p` at index `1` of that list. Other commands may need different interactions with the `Model`.
1. The result of the command execution is encapsulated as a `CommandResult` object which is returned from `Logic`.
Here are the other classes in `Logic` (omitted from the class diagram above) that are used for parsing a user command:

* When called upon to parse a user command, the `AddressBookParser` class creates an `XYZCommandParser` (`XYZ` is a placeholder for the specific command name, e.g., `AddCommandParser`). The parser uses the other classes shown above to parse the user command and create an `XYZCommand` object (e.g., `AddCommand`). The `AddressBookParser` returns that object as a `Command` object.

* All `XYZCommandParser` classes, such as `AddCommandParser` and `DeleteCommandParser`, implement the `Parser` interface so they can be treated similarly where appropriate, for example during testing.
Role-management commands use dedicated parsers and delegate catalog validation and assignment updates to the `Model`.

Candidate command fields and `find` keywords use `ParserUtil.verifyPrintableAscii` before their existing validation. This policy is deliberately parser-only: placing it in model constructors would also reject existing valid non-ASCII addresses or notes during JSON loading. Status values, indexes, and confirmation keywords retain their dedicated checks.

`ArgumentTokenizer.tokenizeWithValidation` checks selected raw prefix values before trimming; otherwise trailing control characters could disappear, and invisible-only notes or tags could be mistaken for clearing requests. `AddressBookParser` preserves trailing argument characters for the same reason. The regular tokenizer remains available for commands outside this policy. Character errors take precedence over duplicate-prefix and field validation after tokenisation; command-specific unsupported-prefix checks can still run first. JSON and CSV serialization continue to escape values independently of this input policy.

* Tabs, line breaks, accented letters, emoji, curly quotes, non-breaking spaces (`U+00A0`), and zero-width spaces (`U+200B`) are rejected, even when copied text looks normal. Use ordinary spaces and straight quotes instead.
* Unsupported characters are checked before surrounding spaces are trimmed or empty values are interpreted as clearing a field. They are not silently removed or replaced.

* Errors identify the field prefix or search input for the unsupported code point, for example: `a/ contains unsupported character U+00A0. Use printable ASCII only (U+0020-U+007E).` Remove or replace that character and retry. Rejected commands leave candidate data unchanged.
* Ordinary spaces around field values are still trimmed. Empty notes and tags can still be cleared as described in the User Guide.

* Status values, candidate indexes, and `clear confirm` retain their own validation rules rather than this character check. Command words and prefix syntax are unchanged; use ordinary spaces before prefixes.

* This restriction applies only to new command input, not loading or exporting existing valid records. Existing non-ASCII text is preserved, but cannot be entered as a `find` keyword under this policy. JSON saving and CSV export retain their existing escaping; quotes and commas do not need to be removed from otherwise valid values.

`ArgumentTokenizer` recognises a prefix after whitespace in any letter case, so users who type `S/Offered` get a status field. In v1.5, the same rule also turned text that only looks like a prefix into a new field: `edit 1 a/Unit N/A` silently renamed the candidate to `A`, and `Unit N/A` could not be saved as an address. The current behaviour is as follows.

* `tokenizeWithValidation`, used by `add`, `edit` and `note`, rejects an upper-case prefix that directly follows a field typed with a lower-case prefix, such as the `N/` in `edit 1 a/Unit N/A` or the `S/` in `edit 1 a/12 Kent Ridge Drive S/Offered`. Either reading is plausible, so the error names the typed prefix, its lower-case form for starting a field, and the escaped form for text in names, phones, emails, addresses or notes. It also states that roles and statuses preserve backslashes. If that prefix is already a field and is not the repeatable `t/` or `r/`, the error omits the duplicate-field option. Name connectors such as `S/O` are removed before the check.

* Multi-field commands remain supported. For successful `add` and `edit` commands, `LogicManager` uses `ArgumentTokenizer.getPrefixWarning` to prepend a warning listing every prefix after the first field, preserving input order, letter case and repetitions. An intentional field update and literal prefix-like text can have identical syntax, so the warning applies to all multi-field commands while preserving one-shot operation. It covers lower-case prefixes as well as upper-case ones, but does not prevent unintended edits. The result is returned only after any required save succeeds; an unchanged edit also carries the warning. Legal-name connectors and escaped slashes are excluded from the prefix list. Single-field edits and other commands retain their existing feedback.

* `tokenizeWithValidation` reads `\/` as `/` in the values it validates: names, phones, emails, addresses, tags and notes. `N\/A` is never matched as a prefix, so it stays in the current value and is saved as `N/A`. Role and status values, including every role command, keep `\/` as typed, so a role saved with `\/` in its name by an earlier version still matches only itself.
* A lower-case prefix inside a value, such as `a/Unit n/a`, still starts a field, as in AB3, and is now included in the warning. The User Guide shows `\/` for keeping that text.

* The rejection, not the `\/` escape alone, is what fixes the silent change. A user who has not read about `\/` would still have `edit 1 a/Unit N/A` rename the candidate; the error stops the edit and shows the escape when it is needed.

`status`, `note`, `expand`, `edit`, and `delete` all read their index with `ParserUtil.parseDisplayedIndex`, so they report numeric index errors the same way. The exact messages are listed under each command in the User Guide. A rejected command leaves candidate data, filters, and the expanded view unchanged.
* A number too large for an `int` is reported as an out-of-range index rather than a format error, because no displayed list can be that long.
* A known numeric problem, such as `0`, is reported instead of the generic `Invalid command format!`, so the user knows exactly what to fix.
* Each command keeps its own validation order. For example, `note` still reports a missing `no/` before an invalid index. This keeps the change limited to index errors.
* stores the address book data i.e., all `Person` objects (which are contained in a `UniquePersonList` object).
* stores a shared role catalog in `AddressBook`, separately from candidate assignments.

* enforces email-only uniqueness through `Person.isSamePerson`, using case-insensitive comparison. `ParserUtil.parseEmail` trims command input, while `Email` validates stored values and preserves case. Full `Person.equals` and `Email.equals` remain case-sensitive. Add, edit, bulk replacement and JSON loading share this identity rule. Edit permits unchanged identity because the list already enforces uniqueness; a changed identity is checked against the entire address book, not only the displayed list.

* stores the `Person` objects selected by the current filter, such as search results, in a separate _filtered_ list. It exposes this list as an unmodifiable `ObservableList<Person>` that the UI can observe and bind to, so the UI updates when the list changes.
* tracks whether the displayed list is in expanded view as transient state. The `Logic` API exposes this read-only property to the `UI`; it is not persisted.
* stores a `UserPrefs` object that represents the user’s preferences (currently, just the GUI settings). This is exposed to the outside as a `ReadOnlyUserPrefs` object.
* does not depend on any of the other three components (as the `Model` represents data entities of the domain, they should make sense on their own without depending on other components)

The catalog stores roles independently of candidates so that unused roles remain available, even after all candidates are cleared. Commands identify roles by name rather than list position, so catalog sorting does not change their targets.

* Each candidate has at least one role from the catalog. `Person` removes `No role` whenever named roles are assigned, including when loading older mixed assignments. The protected `No role` entry provides a fallback when deleting the candidate's last role.
* Roles keep a stable identity across renames. A rename updates the catalog and all assigned candidates together, including candidates outside the displayed list.

* Role lookup keys use Unicode NFC before case conversion; display names and IDs retain their stored values. Catalogs with canonical name collisions are rejected through the existing paired-file backup path, rather than silently merging identities and assignments.

* Parsers validate role names through `ParserUtil.parseRoleName`; commands resolve membership through `RoleCatalog` before changing any data. Person edits replace all assignments in one `setPerson` call.

* `ParserUtil.parseRoleName` also rejects no-break, zero-width and other invisible spaces, because they would let a pasted name look blank or identical to an existing role. As with the printable-ASCII check for candidate fields, this check is parser-only, so catalog entries saved by earlier versions still load.

* Role filters retain IDs rather than `Role` objects because role equality includes the display name. A rename therefore keeps matching the same role; a newly created role with a deleted role's name does not inherit its filter. Status and role groups combine with `AND`, with `OR` within each group.

* `AddressBook` validates a complete catalog and assignment replacement before applying a role rename or deletion, preventing inconsistent references or partial updates. `ModelManager` retains the current filter or reselects the expanded candidate after those domain updates; expanded view requires exactly one displayed candidate.

* `CommandPrefixes` in Commons supplies parameter text to `CliSyntax`, role-name validation and role-management parsers. This keeps reserved syntax consistent without making the model depend on Logic.
* can save both address book data and user preference data in JSON format, and read them back into corresponding objects.
* is implemented by `StorageManager`, which coordinates candidate and role files through `RoleDataStorage` and delegates preference storage to `JsonUserPrefsStorage`.
* depends on some classes in the `Model` component (because the `Storage` component's job is to save/retrieve objects that belong to the `Model`)

`JsonAddressBookStorage` never overwrites the data file in place, so a failed or interrupted save leaves the previous file intact. It writes the JSON to a uniquely named `HRvest-<random>.tmp` file in the same folder, gives it the existing file's access permissions, and then atomically replaces the data file with it. Filesystems that cannot replace a file atomically reject the save, and permission errors abort it; `LogicManager` reports either error. A symbolic link to the data file is kept, and its target is replaced. The temporary file is deleted if the save fails, but a crash or power loss can leave it behind; later saves ignore such files, and they can be deleted once HRvest is closed.

Before loading preferences, recovering files or constructing storage, `MainApp` acquires a `DataDirectoryLock` on `data/.hrvest.lock`. The OS lock is held through preference saving at shutdown and released on failed initialization. This prevents a second process from loading stale candidates and later overwriting newer data, even through a read command that triggers saving. The lock file stays in place after release: deleting it could let two processes lock different files with the same path. Separate data folders remain independent, and process termination releases the OS lock automatically.

During startup, `MainApp` uses the storage component's `CandidateDataInitializer` to load candidate records before creating the UI or command logic. A `DataLoadingException` triggers a persistent, uniquely named `HRvest-<timestamp>-<random>-corrupt.json` backup through `Storage`, followed by a journal-coordinated save of an empty candidate list and the built-in role catalogue. The local-time `yyyyMMddTHHmmss` timestamp makes the newest backup easy to find when several accumulate. The backup copies the original bytes first and then applies the original's supported access restrictions, so a write-restricted data file can still be backed up. An unsuccessful copy removes only its own partial backup where possible. Recovery resolves symbolic links to existing targets; inaccessible files and dangling links are not treated as missing files.

Both backup and replacement saving must finish before commands become available. Otherwise startup shows an actionable error dialog and exits after dismissal, preserving the original and any completed backup. After successful recovery, `UiManager` displays the backup path and restoration instructions. A later launch loads the saved empty file normally, avoiding repeated backups or sample data. Preference-file recovery remains separate.

The activity diagram below summarizes candidate data initialization and recovery. Load failures include malformed JSON, invalid candidate data or role catalog entries, unknown role IDs, and null entries rejected during deserialization or validation.
<puml src="diagrams/DataRecoveryActivityDiagram.puml" alt="Startup candidate data loading and recovery, including backup and replacement save failures" />

Candidates store role IDs, while `roles.json` stores the catalog. `RoleDataStorage` loads the catalog first so that it can validate candidate assignments. Older candidates without role assignments receive `No role`; invalid assignments use the data-recovery process described above.
The two files must stay consistent, but a filesystem rename can replace only one file at a time. To support recovery:
* A rollback journal, `roles-transaction.json`, preserves the previous files before either is replaced. Failed or interrupted saves restore that pair before data is loaded again.

* Invalid journals or incomplete rollback block further saves, preserving the recovery data. Candidate, catalog, and journal paths must identify different files, and concurrent HRvest instances are unsupported.

* Recovery from invalid candidate or catalog data backs up both originals before saving an empty candidate list and the built-in catalog. The catalog backup uses the candidate backup name with `.roles.json` appended; a catalog-only backup is used when no candidate file exists.
* If saving a command fails, `LogicManager` restores the previous model data, filter, and expanded view so that memory and saved data remain consistent after successful rollback.

* `LogicManager` compares the immutable candidate records and role catalog before and after execution. It saves only when persisted data changes, so a storage error cannot block view changes, help, or exit. Import retains its separate save and rollback pipeline, including empty imports.
Classes used by multiple components are in the `seedu.address.commons` package.
This section describes some noteworthy details on how certain features are implemented.
Each candidate has at most one note, such as interview feedback. `note INDEX no/NOTE_TEXT` replaces the note of a candidate in the displayed list, and `note INDEX no/` clears it.

* `Person` holds the note as an `Optional<Note>`. `Note` is an immutable value that rejects blank text and text longer than `Note.MAX_LENGTH` (500) characters, so a candidate either has a valid note or none. `ParserUtil#parseNote` and `JsonAdaptedPerson` trim the text before creating a `Note`.

* `NoteCommandParser` tokenizes the arguments with `no/` as its only prefix, so text such as `n/A` inside a note stays part of the note. It rejects a missing or repeated `no/`. Blank note text creates a `NoteCommand` that clears the note.

* `NoteCommand#execute` finds the candidate in the displayed list and builds a new `Person` with the same details and the new note, because `Person` is immutable. It then calls `Model#setPerson`, which keeps the current filter and keeps the candidate expanded if it was.
* `add` and `edit` reject `no/` through `ParserUtil#verifyNoNotePrefix`, so `note` is the only command that changes a note.
* `JsonAdaptedPerson` stores the note text in a `note` field. On loading, a missing, `null` or blank `note` means no note, so data files from before notes existed still load.
* `PersonCard` shows a sticky-note icon when `Person#hasNote()` is true and shows the note text only in expanded view.
The sequence diagram below shows how `note 2 no/Strong on SQL` is executed. `p` is the candidate at index 2 of the displayed list.
<puml src="diagrams/NoteSequenceDiagram.puml" alt="Interactions inside the Logic and Model components for the note 2 no/Strong on SQL command" />
After the note command returns, `LogicManager` saves the address book if its data changed.
**Aspect: One note or a list of notes**
* **Alternative 1 (current choice):** One note per candidate, replaced by each `note` command.
* Pros: Simple to use and display. No extra commands or indexes are needed to correct or remove one entry.
* Cons: Replacing a note loses the earlier text, so the User Guide tells users to include anything they want to keep.
* **Alternative 2:** A list of notes that `note` appends to.
* Pros: Keeps a full history of interactions with the candidate.
* Cons: Needs commands to edit or delete a single entry, and makes the expanded view longer.
**Aspect: A separate command or a field of `add` and `edit`**
* Pros: The note can contain text that looks like a prefix, because `no/` is the only prefix `note` recognises. An `edit` cannot replace a note by accident.
* Cons: Users learn one more command.
* Cons: Any other prefix inside the note, such as the `a/` in "follow up on a/b test", would start a new field.

The command history feature lets a user walk through commands they submitted earlier in the current session, using the `Up` and `Down` arrow keys. It is implemented as a single collaborator (`CommandHistory`) owned by `CommandBox`.
`CommandBox` already owns the JavaFX `TextField` and runs user input through `CommandExecutor` on Enter. The new field reuses that path:

1. On Enter, `CommandBox#handleCommandEntered` records the raw text with `CommandHistory#add` **before** dispatching to the executor. Rejected commands are recorded too. The text field is cleared after a successful command. After a rejected command, the text stays so that the user can fix it, and `CommandHistory#moveCursorToNewest` marks that entry as already shown, so the next Up press shows the command before it instead of appearing to do nothing.

2. A `KEY_PRESSED` event filter on `commandTextField` catches `UP` and `DOWN` presses, calls `history.previous()` or `history.next()`, and swaps the text field's contents with the result. The event is consumed so the caret does not move within the text field.

3. When the user presses `Up` while composing a fresh command, `CommandBox` captures the current text as a `draft` before replacing the field with a past entry. Pressing `Down` back past the newest entry restores that draft.

`CommandHistory` is a small helper class in the `ui` package. It stores submitted commands in insertion order and tracks a `cursor` that sits at `entries.size()` when the user is composing a fresh command (the "past-the-end" position).

* `add(String)` appends and resets the cursor to the past-the-end position. Blank commands are ignored, and a command identical to the most recent entry is also skipped so repeated submissions do not take up extra slots.
* `previous()` moves the cursor one step back and returns the command there, or `Optional.empty()` when already at the oldest entry.
* `next()` moves the cursor forward. On reaching the past-the-end position it returns an empty string so the UI knows to clear or restore the field.
* Entries are capped at `MAX_ENTRIES` (100) to bound memory for long-running sessions. The oldest entry is dropped when the cap is reached.
* `moveCursorToNewest()` moves the cursor onto the newest entry when the command box keeps a rejected command on screen.

* **Session-only, no persistence.** Keeping history in memory avoids a storage format change for a quality-of-life feature. Command history is session-scoped and is not restored after restarting HRvest.
* **Record failed commands too.** The whole point of Up/Down is to iterate faster; forcing users to retype a mistyped `filtwr s/Interviewing` would defeat that.
* **Hard cap at 100 entries.** Prevents unbounded growth in long sessions. 100 is chosen to be well above the dozen or so commands a typical session uses while still being cheap.
* **Event filter, not handler.** A filter runs before the `TextField`'s own key-handling, so the arrow keys do not also move the caret while cycling.

Import adds a batch of candidates to the complete address book, regardless of the current filter. `AddressBookParser` uses `ImportCommandParser` to create an `ImportCommand`, and `LogicManager` delegates the operation to `ImportOperation`.

`StorageManager` delegates reading `import.csv` to `CsvImportReader`. Missing files and read failures produce an error explaining the problem and expected path. HRvest reads the file into a bounded buffer and parses only that copy; later edits do not affect the buffered data. `CandidateCsvParser` uses `StrictCsvParser` to parse the buffered CSV and validates candidate fields through the existing command/model rules. Import and export share their headers through `CandidateCsvFormat`.

HRvest does not lock the file or check for concurrent changes: these may cause a normal read/validation error or go undetected and import valid-looking altered data. HRvest does not guarantee that bytes read during an external edit represent one consistent file version. Do not externally modify saved JSON or run another HRvest instance against the same saved data during import.

`ImportOperation` checks for duplicates within the batch and against existing candidates before updating the model and saving through storage. It manages its own rollback because import bypasses `LogicManager`'s ordinary save path. Reading or validation failures leave the model unchanged; application or save failures trigger restoration of the previous data and view. Success shows the full candidate list and exits expanded view.

The CSV identifies roles by name, not by catalog ID, because the file may be imported into an HRvest whose catalog has different IDs or lacks those roles. `ImportOperation` passes the current catalog to `CandidateCsvParser`, which matches names as role commands do and creates each unknown name once, so records naming `QA` and `qa` share one new role. `ImportOperation` adds the new roles to the catalog in the same model update and save as the candidates, so a failure rolls both back. Creating roles, rather than rejecting the import as `add` does, lets an export restore on a fresh installation; the success message names the created roles so that a misspelt name is noticed.

Batch combination installs the validated list once, preserving existing and CSV order. `UniquePersonList` checks bulk replacements with a case-insensitive email set instead of comparing every pair. This keeps the same identity rule while avoiding quadratic validation during import, snapshots, and saves.

Failed saves retain the previous saved JSON. If rollback itself fails, HRvest reports that separately; stop using the app and check saved data before restarting. Crash/power-loss recovery is not an in-memory rollback guarantee.
See the [User Guide](UserGuide.md#importing-candidates-import) for import limits and usage restrictions.

**Required CSV template:** UTF-8 with or without a single leading byte order mark (BOM), and exact lowercase headers in the order below. Fields may be unquoted or double-quoted. Fields containing commas or quotes must be double-quoted; double any embedded quotes. Quotes must enclose the entire field, with no extra text or spaces outside the closing quote. Quoting does not bypass field validation. LF (`\n`) and CRLF (`\r\n`) record endings are accepted, and the last record need not end with a newline. Empty trailing lines are allowed, but blank lines before the header or between records, whitespace-only trailing lines, bare CR separators, alternate delimiters, and incorrect column counts are rejected.

Configure your editor to save the example as UTF-8 with LF or CRLF line endings. Excel's optional quoting is accepted when saving as comma-delimited UTF-8 CSV; other encodings or delimiters are not. HRvest accepts the leading BOM written by `export`, so you can copy or rename `data/export.csv` to `data/import.csv` without removing it. The file must still meet validation, duplicate, and resource-limit rules. A BOM-only file or repeated leading BOMs are rejected. Only one encoding marker immediately before the header is ignored; markers inside quoted fields are literal data subject to field validation.

Existing field rules apply, including trimming as in commands. Status accepts defined values ignoring case and surrounding whitespace; empty or unknown statuses fail. Tags must be a JSON array of valid tag-name strings, without nulls, nested values, or trailing JSON. Tags need not be sorted; surrounding whitespace is trimmed, repeated identical names collapse, and `Java` and `java` remain distinct. Roles use the same JSON array form and limits but must name at least one role; names follow the role name rules, and `No role` is dropped when named roles are present, as in `add`. An empty or whitespace-only note means no note. Addresses and notes use their model validation rather than the command-only printable-ASCII check, so supported legacy Unicode data can be exported and imported again. Addresses retain command-style surrounding-space trimming. Nonblank notes are stripped of surrounding whitespace and limited to 500 Unicode code points; tabs, line breaks, and non-ASCII text inside a quoted note are preserved. Formula-like text remains ordinary data where the field permits it; HRvest never executes it.

CSV syntax errors identify the record (the header is record 1) and, for field-specific syntax errors, the one-based field number and name. Messages distinguish missing or extra columns, misplaced or unclosed quotes, content after a closing quote, and unsupported bare CR endings, with guidance on correcting the file. Record numbers count CSV records, not physical lines inside quoted fields.
The `export` command creates a CSV copy of all candidate records, regardless of the current search or filter. It leaves the application's data and current view unchanged.

`ExportCommand` requests an export through `CommandResult`. `LogicManager` passes the complete address book to `StorageManager`, which delegates CSV formatting and writing to `CsvExportWriter`. This keeps file operations in the storage component rather than the model.

The writer exports one row per candidate, with a header and the name, phone, email, address, status, tags, note and roles fields, to `export.csv` beside the JSON data file. The data file path is fixed at `data/HRvest.json`, so the export is always `data/export.csv`. The file starts with a UTF-8 byte order mark so that spreadsheet programs such as Excel detect the encoding; without it, Excel reads the file as ANSI and garbles non-ASCII text. Every field is quoted, embedded quotes are doubled. Literal values, including embedded line breaks, are preserved. Status uses its displayed label; an absent note is empty. Tags occupy one CSV field containing a JSON array, such as `["Java","backend"]`, with CSV escaping applied. Tag names are sorted in case-sensitive Java string order, preserving casing; no tags gives `[]`. Roles use the same form, with names in `list_role` order, ignoring case; a candidate without a named role gives `["No role"]`.

**Spreadsheet caution:** This is raw-data CSV, not a spreadsheet document. Import columns as text to preserve leading zeroes in phone numbers and prevent formula-like stored text from being interpreted as formulas. HRvest does not add sanitisation prefixes or formula wrappers, because they would change the stored values in the file; the User Guide warns users instead. Spreadsheet auto-detection can still alter values when the file is opened directly.

HRvest shows a confirmation after the export completes, or an error if it fails. Export bypasses JSON saving because it does not change candidate data. To protect an earlier CSV snapshot, it writes a temporary sibling file, preserving the destination's existing access permissions, closes and flushes it to disk, then atomically replaces `export.csv`. There is no non-atomic fallback: unsupported atomic replacement fails while retaining the previous CSV. Handled failures attempt to remove the temporary file. If cleanup also fails, the original export failure remains the cause of the reported error, with the cleanup failure attached to it as a suppressed exception. Cleanup failure or process termination may leave the temporary file behind, but cannot expose a partially written replacement as `export.csv`.

Failures display `Export failed:` with the reason and destination when available. Check that the file/folder is writable. Directories, symbolic links (including dangling links), and other non-regular destinations are rejected without deleting them. A missing data directory is created first, as JSON saving does. If the required parent directory cannot be determined or created, export fails. No failure redirects output to another location. Candidate data and the current view remain unchanged. Write, close and replacement failures leave the previous export intact.

* **Candidate**: A person being considered for an open role.
* **Open role**: A position for which the startup is currently recruiting.
* **Role catalog**: The shared collection of roles available in HRvest, including unused roles and the built-in `No role`.
* **Application**: A candidate's consideration for a particular open role, including the candidate status and relevant hiring details.
* **Candidate profile**: The candidate's contact information and hiring details shown together in HRvest.
* **Follow-up**: An action the hiring manager needs to take for a candidate after a prior interaction.
* **Candidate details**: A candidate's name, phone number, email address, address, status, roles and tags.
* **Candidate status**: One of Applied, Shortlisted, Interviewing, Offered, Accepted, Rejected, or Withdrawn.

* **Duplicate candidate**: A candidate with the same email address as another candidate in HRvest, compared case-insensitively after trimming command input. No other fields, including name, status, roles, tags or notes, affect duplicate detection.
* **Mainstream OS**: Windows, Linux, Unix, or macOS
* **Note**: A single text remark about a candidate, such as interview feedback or follow-up context.

HRvest is a **desktop address book that helps hiring managers at startups track candidates through the hiring pipeline with less administrative work**. While it has a GUI (Graphical User Interface), most interactions are short typed commands in a CLI (Command Line Interface), so if you type fast, you can work faster than in a mouse-driven applicant tracking system.
1. Ensure that Java `25` or later is installed on your computer.
**Mac users:** Ensure you have the precise JDK version prescribed [here](https://se-education.org/guides/tutorials/javaInstallationMac.html).
1. Copy the file to the folder you want to use as the _home folder_ for HRvest.
1. Open a terminal, `cd` to the folder containing the JAR file, and run `java -jar HRvest.jar`.

A GUI similar to the one below should appear in a few seconds, listing some sample candidates. The screenshot shows a different set of candidates, filtered with `filter s/Shortlisted s/Interviewing s/Offered`.
1. Type a command in the command box and press Enter to execute it. For example, type **`help`** and press Enter to open the help window.
Some example commands you can try:
* `add n/John Doe p/98765432 e/johnd@example.com a/John street, block 123, #01-01 r/No role` : Adds a candidate named `John Doe` to HRvest.
* `delete 3` : Deletes the 3rd candidate shown in the current list.
* `clear confirm` : Deletes all candidates. `clear` on its own only asks you to confirm.
1. Refer to the [Features](#features) section below for details of each command.
* Words in `UPPER_CASE` are the parameters to be supplied by the user.
For example, in `add n/NAME`, replace `NAME` with a value such as `John Doe`.
* Items in square brackets are optional.
For example, `n/NAME [t/TAG]` can be used as `n/John Doe t/friend` or as `n/John Doe`.
* Items followed by `...` can appear zero or more times.
For example, `[t/TAG]... ` may be omitted, or written as `t/friend` or `t/friend t/family`.
* Command words and prefixes ignore letter case.
For example, `LIST` is read the same way as `list`, and `S/Offered` the same way as `s/Offered`.
* To keep text that looks like a prefix, such as `N/A`, inside a value, type `\/` for its slash.

For example, `edit 1 a/Unit N\/A` sets the address to `Unit N/A`. This works in names, phone numbers, emails, addresses, tags and notes, where every `\/` you type is saved as `/`. Role names and statuses keep backslashes literally. To assign an existing role named `N/A`, use `edit 1 r/N/A` with no space after `r/`; `r/ N/A` is ambiguous, and `r/N\/A` refers to a different role whose name contains a backslash.

* In `add`, `edit` and `note`, an upper-case prefix that follows a lower-case one, such as the `N/` in `edit 1 a/Unit N/A`, could be either text or a new field, so HRvest rejects the command and changes nothing. The error offers `n/` to start a field and `N\/` for literal text in names, phones, emails, addresses or notes. If the field is already supplied and cannot be repeated, as in `edit 1 n/Bob a/Unit N/A`, it does not offer another `n/` field. Escaping does not bypass the field's validation rules.

* Successful `add` and `edit` commands with multiple fields show a warning before the success message, listing every prefix after the first field in input order, including lower-case and repeated prefixes. For example, `edit 1 A/Unit N/A` changes the address to `Unit` and the name to `A`, with `Warning: Prefixes read as additional fields: N/.` Likewise, `edit 1 a/Unit n/a` changes the address to `Unit` and the name to `a`, with a warning listing `n/`. The command is applied and saved immediately; this warning does not ask for confirmation or prevent an unintended edit. Check the updated candidate details.

* The warning also appears for intentional multi-field commands and unchanged edits. For example, `edit 1 A/Unit P/123 N/A` lists both `P/` and `N/`. A single-field edit produces no prefix warning. Escaped text and legal-name connectors are not listed as extra fields: `edit 1 A/Unit N\/A` saves the complete address without warning. Use `edit 1 a/Unit n\/a` to keep lower-case `n/a` in the address.
* Parameters can be in any order.

For example, if the command specifies `n/NAME p/PHONE_NUMBER`, `p/PHONE_NUMBER n/NAME` is also acceptable. The only exception is `INDEX`, which must come right after the command word: `status 2 s/Offered` works, but `status s/Offered 2` does not.
* Extraneous parameters for `help`, `list`, `exit`, `export`, and `import` are ignored.
For example, `help 123` is interpreted as `help`. `clear` accepts only `confirm`, and the `list_role` command rejects all arguments.

* If you are using a PDF version of this document, be careful when copying and pasting commands that span multiple lines as space characters surrounding line-breaks may be omitted when copied over to the application.

After `edit`, `note`, or `status`, the current name search, status filter, or role filter stays active. Candidates that no longer match disappear from the displayed list, so displayed indexes may change.

`expand` replaces that filter with a selection of one candidate at index `1`. Updating the expanded candidate keeps them selected at index `1`, even if their new details would not match the earlier filter.
Check the displayed list before using another index command. Use `list` to show all candidates again.

Names, phone numbers, emails, addresses, tags, notes, and `find` keywords accept only **printable ASCII (`U+0020–U+007E`)**: English letters (`A–Z`, `a–z`), digits (`0–9`), ordinary spaces, and ASCII punctuation. This keeps command input within a single, explicit character set. Existing field rules still apply afterward: for example, phone numbers need at least three ASCII digits, and names accept only the punctuation used in legal names, such as `O'Brien`, `Jr.`, `s/o` and `(Kelvin)`.

For more information about rejected characters, error messages, and validation scope, see [Command input character validation in the Developer Guide](DeveloperGuide.md#command-input-character-validation).
Shows a message explaining how to access the help page.
Format: `add n/NAME p/PHONE_NUMBER e/EMAIL a/ADDRESS r/ROLE [r/MORE_ROLE]... [s/STATUS] [t/TAG]... `
| Parameter | Required? | Accepted values and behavior |
| `n/NAME` | Yes | A non-blank, printable-ASCII name that follows the [Name rules](#name-rules), e.g. `n/John Doe`. See below for punctuation, markers and parameter-ordering guidance. |

| `p/PHONE_NUMBER` | Yes | Any printable-ASCII text containing at least three ASCII digits, e.g. `p/+65 9123 4567`, `p/(65) 6123 4567`, or `p/1234 5678 (HP) 1111-3333 (Office)`. Formatting, extensions and contact labels are accepted. Leading and trailing spaces are removed; internal text and leading zeroes are preserved. HRvest stores contact information without checking whether a number is dialable. |

| `e/EMAIL` | Yes | An address in `local-part@domain` format, e.g. `e/anne.o'brien@example.com`. The local part allows letters, digits, and !#$%&'*+/=?^_`{|}~-, with periods separating non-empty groups. Leading, trailing, and consecutive periods are invalid. Domain labels must start and end with letters or digits and may contain internal hyphens, including consecutive hyphens (e.g. `xn--bcher-kva.de`); the final label must contain at least two characters. Spaces and quoted local parts are not accepted. |
| `a/ADDRESS` | Yes | Any non-blank, printable-ASCII address, e.g. `a/John street, block 123, #01-01`. Spaces and punctuation are allowed. |
| `r/ROLE` | Yes | An existing [role name](#managing-the-role-catalog). Repeat `r/` to assign multiple roles. Matching ignores case and surrounding whitespace. Use `r/No role` if no role applies. |

| `s/STATUS` | No | One of `Applied`, `Shortlisted`, `Interviewing`, `Offered`, `Accepted`, `Rejected`, or `Withdrawn`. Defaults to `Applied` if omitted. Input ignores letter case, so `s/interviewing` is saved and displayed as `Interviewing`. A bare `s/` is invalid rather than using the default. |

| `t/TAG` | No | A non-blank printable ASCII label, including punctuation and internal spaces, e.g. `t/C++`, `t/C#`, `t/.NET`, `t/Node.js`, or `t/machine learning`. Surrounding spaces are trimmed; internal spaces are preserved. Repeat the prefix for multiple tags: `t/C++ t/machine learning`. Tags are case-sensitive: `t/Java` and `t/java` are distinct. Omit `t/` for no tags; a bare `t/` is invalid when adding. A recognized command prefix preceded by a space starts another field, even inside a tag: `t/machine learning n/Alice` sets the tag to `machine learning` and the name to `Alice`. Quoting does not escape prefixes. Slashes without a preceding prefix boundary are allowed, e.g. `t/C/C++`. |
These rules apply to names supplied through `add` and `edit`.
* **Punctuation between letters or digits:** Apostrophes, periods, hyphens and slashes are accepted, e.g. `Anne O'Brien`, `J.R. Tan`, `Kelly-Ann Tan` and `Ravi s/o Kumar`.

* **Other legal-name forms:** A word may end with one period (`Tan Ah Kow Jr.`). A comma may follow a word or closing parenthesis, but must be followed by a space and another word (`Martin Luther King, Jr.` or `Tan (Kelvin), Jr.`); a trailing comma is rejected. Parenthesised words are accepted after the first word (`Tan Wei Ming (Kelvin)`), and a separate `@` may introduce an alias (`Mohamed Ali @ Ahmad`). Parentheses must enclose complete words without spaces immediately inside them; `@` needs a name on both sides.

* **Name markers:** Accepted examples include `s/o`, `d/o`, `a/l`, `a/p` and `l/p`; slashes between letters or digits are not limited to these markers. Within a name, `s/o` followed by a space stays part of the name rather than starting a status field, regardless of letter case. `d/o` and `l/p` stay part of the name because `d/` and `l/` are not command prefixes. The markers `a/l` and `a/p` can resemble an address field and require the ordering below.

* **Ordering names and addresses:** When using `a/l` or `a/p` in a name, put the address first, e.g. `edit 1 a/1 Road n/Siti a/p Ahmad`. A later address is also accepted if another field, such as `p/`, separates it from the name.

* **Ambiguous addresses:** An address beginning with `L` or `P` can look like a name marker. Put the address first, e.g. `edit 1 a/L Street n/John`. An ambiguous sequence such as `edit 1 n/John a/L Street a/9 Road` is rejected rather than guessed.
* **Rejected punctuation:** Other punctuation, repeated punctuation such as `O''Brien`, and punctuation-only words are rejected.

* **Characters and spacing:** Only [printable ASCII](#accepted-characters-in-candidate-inputs) is accepted. Enter accented or non-Latin names such as `José` or `陈` in romanised form, e.g. `Jose`. Leading and trailing spaces are removed; internal spaces and letter case are preserved.
* Supply each of `n/`, `p/`, `e/`, `a/`, and `s/` at most once. Both `t/` and `r/` can be repeated. Repeated single-valued prefixes are rejected, even if their values are identical.

* The error message lists all missing required parameters together, including `r/ROLE`. If the role is missing, it also explains that you can use `r/No role` if no role applies. For example, bare `add` reports `Missing n/NAME, p/PHONE_NUMBER, e/EMAIL, a/ADDRESS, r/ROLE. Use r/No role if no role applies.` The command `add n/John Doe r/No role` reports `Missing p/PHONE_NUMBER, e/EMAIL, a/ADDRESS.`
* Create named roles with `add_role` before assigning them to a candidate. A bare `r/` or an unknown role is rejected.

* Email alone identifies duplicates: surrounding whitespace is trimmed and the whole email is compared case-insensitively. For example, `Alice@Example.com` and `alice@example.com` belong to the same candidate. Adding a duplicate is rejected with `Another candidate (NAME) already uses this email.`, where `NAME` identifies the matching existing record, even if hidden by a filter. The submitted candidate and current view are not changed. Names, phones, addresses, statuses, roles, tags, and notes do not affect duplicate detection. Candidates with the same name but different emails are allowed. Email capitalisation is preserved for display and storage.

* Use only the documented prefixes. Unknown prefixes such as `x/` are treated as part of the preceding value, not as separate fields. A recognised prefix preceded by whitespace starts a new field, even if you intended it to be part of an address: `a/Unit n/a` sets the name to `a`. An upper-case prefix after a lower-case one, such as the `T/` in `a/Unit T/2`, is rejected rather than guessed. To keep such text, type `\/` for its slash: `a/Unit T\/2` saves the address `Unit T/2`. The only exceptions are the name connectors `s/o`, `a/l` and `a/p` within `n/NAME`, described in [Name rules](#name-rules) above.

* `no/` is reserved for the `note` command and is rejected anywhere in `add`, in any letter case, including with empty text or after a tab. The error is `The add command does not support no/. Add the candidate first, then use note INDEX no/NOTE_TEXT.` Add the candidate without `no/`, then use their displayed index with `note` to record a note. Text such as `yes/no/feedback` inside an address word remains literal address text.
* `add n/John Doe p/98765432 e/johnd@example.com a/John street, block 123, #01-01 r/No role`
* `add n/Betsy Crowe p/1234567 e/betsy@example.com a/Newgate Prison r/Developer s/Interviewing t/backend` (create `Developer` first with `add_role n/Developer`).
Shows a list of all candidates in HRvest, along with the total count.
* The success message is `Listed all N candidate(s).`, where `N` is the current number of candidates. For example, `Listed all 6 candidate(s).`
* If HRvest has no candidates, the message is `There are no candidates yet. Use add to add one.`
Edits an existing candidate in HRvest.
The success message shows the candidate's updated details.
* Edits the candidate at the specified `INDEX`. The index refers to the index number shown in the displayed candidate list. The index **must be a positive integer** 1, 2, 3, ...
* At least one of the optional fields must be provided.
* Existing values will be updated to the input values.
* Keeps the current filter or expanded view. See [Filters and expanded view](#filters-and-expanded-view) for details.
* If every value you give matches the candidate's current details, nothing is changed and the message is `No changes made: NAME already has these details.`

* An email matching another candidate's email (ignoring case and surrounding whitespace) is rejected with `Another candidate (NAME) already uses this email.`, where `NAME` identifies the matching existing record rather than the submitted name, even if hidden by a filter. The original candidate, filter, and expanded view remain unchanged. Keeping your candidate's email, changing only its capitalisation, or editing other fields does not cause a self-duplicate error.

* Supplied `r/` values replace all existing roles; omitting `r/` preserves them. A bare `r/` is invalid; use `r/No role` to remove named roles. Unknown roles suggest `add_role n/NAME`, and an invalid role leaves all details unchanged.
* When editing tags, all of the candidate's existing tags are removed; adding tags is not cumulative.
* To remove all of a candidate's tags, enter `t/` without a tag after it.

* As in `add`, a recognised prefix after a space starts a new field, and an upper-case prefix after a lower-case one is rejected. For example, `edit 1 a/Unit N/A` reports that `N/` could be text or the `n/` prefix, and changes nothing. Use `edit 1 a/Unit N\/A` to set the address to `Unit N/A`. Check the success message, which shows the updated details.

* To avoid confusing an address beginning with `L` or `P` with a legal-name marker, put the address first, e.g. `edit 1 a/L Street n/John` or `edit 1 a/9 Road n/Siti a/p Ahmad`. An ambiguous sequence such as `edit 1 n/John a/L Street a/9 Road` is rejected without changing the candidate.

* `edit` does not change notes. Like `add`, it rejects `no/` anywhere, in any letter case, with `The edit command does not support no/. Use note INDEX no/NOTE_TEXT to add, replace or clear a note.` Use the `note` command instead.
*  `edit 1 p/91234567 e/johndoe@example.com` Edits the phone number and email address of the 1st candidate to be `91234567` and `johndoe@example.com` respectively.
*  `edit 2 n/Betsy Crower t/` Edits the name of the 2nd candidate to be `Betsy Crower` and clears all existing tags.
*  `edit 3 s/Offered` Updates the status of the 3rd candidate to `Offered`.
* `edit 1 r/Developer r/Designer` Replaces the 1st candidate's roles with Developer and Designer, which must already exist.
### Adding, replacing, or clearing a candidate's note: `note`
Adds a note to the specified candidate, such as interview feedback or follow-up context.
* Adds the note to the candidate at the specified `INDEX`. The index refers to the index number shown in the displayed candidate list. The index **must be a positive integer** 1, 2, 3, ...

* `0` or a negative index gives `Index must be a positive integer.` An index beyond the displayed list gives `The candidate index provided is invalid.` A missing or non-numeric index gives `Invalid command format!`. The current view stays unchanged.
* Each candidate has one note. If the candidate already has a note, it is replaced by the new note.

* To clear the note, enter `note INDEX no/` with no text after `no/`. Text containing only ordinary spaces also clears the note. The message is `Cleared note for NAME`. Clearing a candidate who already has no note succeeds and keeps that candidate unchanged.

* Non-empty `NOTE_TEXT` can contain at most 500 printable-ASCII characters. Leading and trailing ordinary spaces are removed; spacing, capitalisation, and ASCII punctuation within the note are kept. Tabs, line breaks, and non-ASCII characters are rejected.
* Supply `no/` only once. A later ` no/` or ` NO/` in the text is rejected as a second `no/`; type `no\/` to keep that text in the note. Other prefixes, such as `n/`, are treated as part of the note.
* Keeps the current filter or expanded view. See [Filters and expanded view](#filters-and-expanded-view) for details.
* When adding or replacing a note, the message is `Updated note for NAME: NOTE_TEXT`.
* Editing a candidate or updating their status keeps their note. Use `expand INDEX` to view the full note.
* `note 2 no/Strong on system design, weak on SQL`
* `note 2 no/` clears the 2nd displayed candidate's note. The note icon disappears; expanding the candidate shows `No note recorded.`
* `find Betsy` followed by `note 1 no/Follow up next week` adds a note to the 1st candidate in the results of the `find` command.
Replacing or removing a note deletes the previous note permanently. To keep earlier information, include it in the new note.
Updates the candidate at the given index in the currently displayed list.
* `INDEX` is a positive, 1-based index in the displayed list.
* Valid statuses are `Applied`, `Shortlisted`, `Interviewing`, `Offered`, `Accepted`, `Rejected`, and `Withdrawn`, regardless of letter case.

* Candidates created with `add` start with `Applied` unless an initial `s/STATUS` is supplied. Status is saved immediately, shown on the candidate card, and does not affect duplicate checking. Older records without a saved status load as `Applied`; explicitly saved statuses are preserved.
* Keeps the current filter or expanded view. See [Filters and expanded view](#filters-and-expanded-view) for details.
* The message is `Updated status of NAME: OLD_STATUS -> NEW_STATUS`.
* If the candidate already has the requested status, the message is `No change: NAME already has status STATUS.` Their record and the current filtered or expanded view stay unchanged.

* `0` or a negative index gives `Index must be a positive integer.` An index beyond the displayed list gives `The candidate index provided is invalid.` A missing or non-numeric index, or a missing `s/`, gives `Invalid command format!`. The candidate and current view stay unchanged.

* An unknown status gives `Status must be one of: Applied, Shortlisted, Interviewing, Offered, Accepted, Rejected, Withdrawn`; repeated `s/` gives `Multiple values specified for the following single-valued field(s): s/`.
Finds candidates with a word in their name that starts with any of the given keywords.
* The search is case-insensitive; for example, `hans` matches `Hans`.
* Keyword order does not matter; for example, `Hans Bo` matches `Bo Hans`.

* The search considers only names. Parentheses and commas in names and keywords are ignored, so both `find Kelvin` and `find (Kelvin)` match `Tan Wei Ming (Kelvin)`, and `find King,` matches `Martin Luther King, Jr.`. Keywords containing only parentheses and commas match no candidates.
* A keyword matches the start of any word in a name; for example, `Han` matches `Hans`, and `Gru` matches `Hans Gruber`. Text inside a word does not match; for example, `ans` does not match `Hans`.
* Candidates matching at least one keyword are returned (an `OR` search); for example, `Hans Bo` returns `Hans Gruber` and `Bo Yang`.

* Each `find` replaces the previous search or filter and considers all candidates, so `find` and `filter` cannot be combined. For example, `filter s/Interviewing` followed by `find Alex` shows every candidate matching `Alex`, whatever their status.
### Filtering candidates by status or role: `filter`
Filters candidates by hiring status, assigned roles, or both.
* Supply at least one status or role.
* Repeat `s/` or `r/` to match any value within that field (`OR`). Repeated values have no extra effect.
* If both fields are supplied, candidates must match a specified status and a specified role (`AND`).

* Each `filter` replaces the previous search or filter and considers all candidates, so `filter` and `find` cannot be combined. For example, `find Alex` followed by `filter r/Developer` shows every Developer, not only those matching `Alex`.
* Status and role matching ignore case. Role names ignore surrounding whitespace and must exist in the catalog.

* Invalid input leaves the displayed list unchanged. An invalid status lists valid statuses; an unknown role suggests `list_role`. Other prefixes are rejected. For example, `filter n/Alex` gives `The filter command does not support n/. Use only s/STATUS and r/ROLE.`
* If no candidates match, the result count is zero.
* Renaming a role keeps an active filter following that role. Deleting it removes that role's matches.
* `filter s/Interviewing s/Offered` shows candidates who are interviewing or have been offered a job.
* `filter r/Developer r/Designer` shows candidates assigned to either role.
* `filter r/Developer s/Interviewing s/Offered` shows Developers who are interviewing or have been offered a job.
* `filter r/No role` shows candidates with no named role.
Deletes the specified candidate from HRvest.
The success message shows the deleted candidate's details, including their status.
* Deletes the candidate at the specified `INDEX`.
* The index refers to the index number shown in the displayed candidate list.
* The index **must be a positive integer** 1, 2, 3, ...
* After `expand`, deleting the expanded candidate shows all remaining candidates again.
* `list` followed by `delete 2` deletes the 2nd candidate in HRvest.
* `find Betsy` followed by `delete 1` deletes the 1st candidate in the results of the `find` command.
Shows the specified candidate's full record, including their full note.
* Shows the candidate at the specified `INDEX`.
* The index refers to the index number shown in the displayed candidate list.
* The index **must be a positive integer** 1, 2, 3, ... within the displayed list.
* `0` or a negative index gives `Index must be a positive integer.` A non-numeric index gives `Invalid index! Index must be a positive integer.` The current view stays unchanged.

* An index beyond the displayed list gives `No candidate found with that index. Enter an index between 1 and N.`, where `N` is the number of candidates shown. A number above 2147483647 gives `The candidate index provided is invalid.`
* The list shows only the selected candidate at index `1`, with their full note. If the candidate has no note, it shows `No note recorded.` Run `list` to show all candidates again.
* If HRvest has no candidates, the error is `There are no candidates yet. Use add to add one.` If only the displayed list is empty, use `list` or change the filter to display candidates.
* `list` followed by `expand 1` shows the 1st candidate in HRvest.
* `filter s/Interviewing` followed by `expand 2` shows the 2nd candidate in the results of the `filter` command.
The role catalog is the shared collection of roles available in HRvest, including unused roles and the built-in `No role`.
* Each candidate has one or more roles. `add` requires explicit roles; create named roles before assigning them, or use `r/No role`.
* `No role` cannot be renamed or deleted. Assigning any named role removes `No role`, even if both are supplied. It remains the fallback when deleting a candidate's last named role.
* Named roles appear as purple badges, `No role` as a red badge, and tags as blue badges. Long role names wrap.
* Unused roles remain available, including after `clear` and restarts.
* Role command words and prefixes are case-insensitive. Put whitespace before each prefix and supply each required prefix exactly once.
* Changes save automatically. Invalid commands report an error without changing candidates or roles.
* Names must not be blank or contain control characters such as tabs or newlines. Punctuation and Unicode characters are accepted.
* Invisible characters, such as no-break spaces (`U+00A0`) and zero-width spaces (`U+200B`), are rejected, even when text copied from a web page looks normal. Use ordinary spaces instead.
* Matching ignores surrounding whitespace and letter case: ` Software Engineer ` matches `software engineer`. Capitalisation is preserved for display.

* Matching also treats canonically equivalent Unicode spellings as the same name: `Café` with a single accented letter matches `Cafe` followed by a combining acute accent. Display spelling and role IDs are preserved. This applies to creation, assignment, filtering, renaming, and deletion.
* Internal spaces matter: `Software  Engineer` (two spaces) is distinct from `Software Engineer`.

* A space followed by `n/`, `r/`, `p/`, `e/`, `a/`, `t/`, `no/`, or `s/` is reserved command syntax, ignoring case. It cannot appear within a role name, and quotes do not escape it. A `\/` in a role name is kept as typed rather than read as `/`.
Creates a role without assigning it to a candidate.
* The name must not match an existing role, including `No role`.
Renames a role for every assigned candidate, including those outside the displayed list.
* The role must exist and must not be `No role`.
* The new name must not match another role. Changing only capitalisation is allowed.
* Keeps the current filter or expanded view. See [Filters and expanded view](#filters-and-expanded-view) for details.
Example: `edit_role r/Software Engineer n/Senior Software Engineer`
Removes a role from the catalog and all assigned candidates.
* The role must exist and must not be `No role`.
* Candidates keep their other roles. Those losing their last role receive `No role`.
* Keeps the current filter or expanded view. See [Filters and expanded view](#filters-and-expanded-view) for details.
Shows all role names in the command result, including unused roles and `No role`.
* Names are sorted alphabetically, ignoring case.
* Accepts no arguments and keeps the candidate filter unchanged.
* The result area grows to show more role names while leaving space for candidate cards. Large catalogs and long names remain scrollable.
Clears all candidates from HRvest while preserving the role catalog, including unused roles.
* `clear` on its own deletes nothing. It shows how many candidates would be deleted and asks you to enter `clear confirm`.
* `clear confirm` deletes every candidate, including those hidden by the current `find` or `filter`. The message is `All candidates have been cleared.`
* `confirm` ignores letter case. Any other text after `clear` is rejected.
* If there are no candidates, both forms reply `There are no candidates to clear.`

Exports every candidate to `data/export.csv`, next to the candidate data file `data/HRvest.json` in the folder you run HRvest from. Candidates are exported in address-book order, regardless of the current search or filter. Candidate data, the current filter, and expanded view remain unchanged.
* The destination is always `data/export.csv`. You are not able to specify your own export path.
* If the data folder does not exist yet (for example, before HRvest has saved any data), `export` creates it.
* The CSV has the columns `name,phone,email,address,status,tags,note,roles`, in that order. Unused roles are not exported; back up both JSON files to keep the complete role catalog.
* The file is UTF-8 with a byte order mark, so spreadsheet programs such as Excel show accented and non-Latin text correctly.

* For example, the tags `Java` and `backend` appear as `["Java","backend"]` in the tags column when the CSV is opened in a spreadsheet. Roles appear the same way, in `list_role` order, such as `["Designer","Developer"]`, or `["No role"]` for a candidate without a named role.
* Success displays `Exported successfully to PATH.`, with the absolute destination, only after writing and closing the file succeeds.
* If the address book is empty, `export` succeeds and writes only the header row, with no candidate rows.
**Opening the CSV in a spreadsheet:** The CSV holds your data exactly as stored, but spreadsheet programs change some values when you double-click to open the file:
* Phone numbers lose their leading zeroes, for example `007` becomes `7`.
* Text that starts with `=`, `+`, `-` or `@`, such as an address `=1+2`, is treated as a formula and calculated.

To keep every value as stored, import the file instead. In Excel, use **Data > From Text/CSV**, choose **Transform Data**, and set the columns to **Text** before loading. Do not open exports from untrusted data with formulas enabled.

**Overwrite warning:** Each successful `export` replaces any existing `export.csv` without asking for confirmation or keeping a backup. Copy or rename the CSV before exporting again if you need to retain that snapshot. HRvest writes and closes a temporary file before atomically replacing the destination. A failed write or replacement leaves the previous CSV intact; a filesystem that cannot replace files atomically reports an export error. An interrupted export may leave a `HRvest-export-*.tmp` file in the data folder; after closing HRvest, you may delete that temporary file.

The **HRvest** text logo appears above the command box. When the window is wide enough, as it is when HRvest first opens on most screens, a row beside it shows **Total candidates** and one card for each recruitment status: Applied, Shortlisted, Interviewing, Offered, Accepted, Rejected, and Withdrawn.

* Each card shows **shown / total**: the number in the currently displayed candidate list versus the number among all candidates loaded in HRvest. For example, `2 / 8` on Interviewing means two interviewing candidates are currently shown, out of eight overall.
* Searching, filtering, or expanding a candidate changes the shown counts; overall counts still include candidates hidden from the list. Use `list` to show all candidates again.
* Adding, updating, deleting, or clearing candidates updates the counts automatically. Statuses with no candidates still have a card, and an empty data set shows `0 / 0` on every card.

* The cards appear together on one row only when every card fits at its minimum width. If the window is too narrow, the entire row disappears while the logo stays visible. Widen the window to restore all cards with up-to-date counts.
The line above the candidate list shows how many candidates are displayed, so you can tell when some are hidden rather than deleted:

* `Showing 2 of 6 candidates (filtered). Type list to show all.` when `find`, `filter`, or a later update to a filtered list hides some candidates.

The command box remembers every command you submit in the current session so you can re-run or edit a past command without retyping it.
* `Up` moves back through your submitted commands. Repeated presses walk further into the past; the earliest entry stays shown once you reach it.
* `Down` moves forward. Pressing past the newest entry restores whatever draft you were typing before you started navigating, or clears the box if there was no draft.

* Both successful and rejected commands are recorded. A rejected command also stays in the command box, shown in red, so you can fix a typo and press Enter again; `Up` then shows the command before it. A command identical to the most recent one does not take up an extra slot.
* Blank submissions are skipped. History is session-scoped and holds up to the 100 most recent commands. Repeating an earlier command that is not the most recent one takes another slot.

HRvest automatically saves data after each command that changes candidates or the role catalog, and after every successful import. Viewing, searching, filtering, help, exit, and commands that leave the stored data unchanged do not rewrite the data files. Use [`export`](#exporting-candidates-export) to create a CSV copy.
